title: SIMD vectorization
description: What SIMD is, what it gains, and which conditions a loop must meet to be vectorized efficiently: programs f0, f2, f3 and f4 with their SIMD versions (4 lanes of 16 bytes) on processor B4. Ends with an exercise: vectorize a loop by hand.

tutorial.name: Lesson L2: SIMD vectorization
tutorial.description: SIMD: what it is, what it gains, and when it pays off

steps.title: SIMD: one instruction, several data
steps.description:
A SIMD instruction (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) operates on a vector register
that holds several elements, its lanes. With 16-byte registers, an instruction
loads, adds or multiplies 4 floats (or 2 doubles) at once.

In this lesson you compare loops with their SIMD versions on processor {{processor}}, with N = {{N}},
and you finish by vectorizing a loop by hand. The bar above counts your tasks.

steps.title: The scalar loop f0
steps.description:
f0 computes C[x] = A[x] + L·B[x] (hover the header to see the C code).
Each iteration processes one element with 8 instructions. Simulate it (▶ Show me) and look at
the port usage: P0 executes every load and store, 3 memory accesses per element,
so f0 cannot go below 3 cycles per element. Now: {{cyclesPerAlgOp}} cycles per element.

steps.title: Task 1: predict f0-SIMD
steps.description:
f0-SIMD is the same loop vectorized with 4 lanes: two vector loads, a vector multiply,
a vector add and a vector store per iteration, and x = x + 4: each iteration does
4 algorithmic operations (S = {{stride}}, shown next to N).
It has the same number of instructions per iteration as f0.
Predict its cycles per algorithmic operation (cycles per element), save it, and simulate.

steps.title: What SIMD gains
steps.description:
f0-SIMD needs {{cyclesPerAlgOp}} cycles per element, about 4 times less than f0.
• Fewer instructions: Instr/Alg Oper drops from 8 to 2. Dispatch, ports and retire
   do the same work per instruction, but each instruction now does 4 times more.
• The bottleneck is still P0 ({{port.P0}}% busy): 3 vector accesses per iteration,
   now for 4 elements.
• Cycles/Alg Oper compares the versions; Cycles/iter does not (an iteration does more work).

steps.title: Task 2: why ×4?
steps.questionText: f0-SIMD runs about 4 times faster than f0 on {{processor}}. Why?

answers.text: Each iteration has the same instructions and takes about the same cycles, but processes 4 elements instead of 1
answers.explanation: Yes: the bottleneck (3 memory accesses on P0) is the same per iteration, and an iteration now covers 4 elements.

answers.text: Vector instructions have a lower latency than scalar ones
answers.explanation: No: on B4 a vector load takes 5 cycles and a scalar one 4; latency is not what limits f0.

answers.text: The SIMD version uses 4 times more ports
answers.explanation: No: both versions use the same ports; P0 is the bottleneck in both.

answers.text: The SIMD version executes 4 times fewer iterations, each 4 times faster
answers.explanation: There are 4 times fewer iterations, but each one takes about the same cycles (≈3), not 4 times fewer.

steps.title: When does vectorization pay off?
steps.description:
f0 is the ideal case. A loop is vectorized efficiently when:
• its iterations are independent: lanes compute different iterations at the same time;
• its accesses are contiguous (stride 1): one vector load brings 4 consecutive elements;
• all its data have the same size: a 16-byte register holds 4 floats but only 2 doubles;
• there are enough iterations (here N = {{N}}, a multiple of 4).
The next examples break one condition each: f2, f3 and f4.

steps.title: f2: a strided access
steps.description:
f2 computes C[x] = A[2x] + B[x]: A is read with stride 2 (one element of every two).
The 4 elements A[2x], A[2x+2], A[2x+4], A[2x+6] are spread over 8 floats:
f2-SIMD needs two vector loads of A and a shuffle that picks the even lanes.
Now 4 vector accesses go through P0 per iteration instead of 3.

steps.title: Task 3: predict f2-SIMD
steps.description:
Scalar f2 takes about 3 cycles per element (3 memory accesses on P0).
Predict the cycles per element of f2-SIMD, with 4 vector accesses per iteration of 4 elements.
Save your prediction and simulate.

steps.title: f3: mixed data sizes
steps.description:
f3 computes C[x] = A[x] + L·B[x] with L double: each float is converted to double,
operated, and converted back to float.
A 16-byte register holds 4 floats but only 2 doubles: f3-SIMD works in halves of 2 lanes,
with conversions, a shuffle, and even stores and loads through the stack (STK) to move the upper half.
It needs 23 instructions per iteration of 4 elements. Simulate it (▶ Show me).

steps.title: Task 4: why so little gain?
steps.questionText: f3 takes about 3.2 cycles per element and f3-SIMD about {{cyclesPerAlgOp}}: a speedup of only about 1.3. Which reasons explain it?

answers.text: Each double vector instruction processes only 2 elements
answers.explanation: Yes: with doubles, the 16-byte registers hold half as many lanes.

answers.text: The conversions and the data moves add instructions that the scalar loop also needs only once per element
answers.explanation: Yes: f3-SIMD needs 23 instructions per 4 elements (5.75 per element) against 11 per element of f3: half the instructions, not a quarter.

answers.text: P0 and P1 are both saturated: the extra loads/stores (STK) and the conversions fill them
answers.explanation: Yes: the throughput bound is 9 cycles per iteration on P0 and on P1.

answers.text: The iterations of f3 depend on each other
answers.explanation: No: the iterations of f3 are independent, as in f0.

steps.title: f4: dependent iterations
steps.description:
f4 computes C[x+1] = C[x] + A[x]·B[x]: each result needs the previous one (a prefix sum).
In the program, the running value is kept in s: s = s + a is a cyclic chain across iterations
(Static Analysis: chain s → s). The 4 lanes would need 4 consecutive results at once,
but each one depends on the previous: a compiler cannot vectorize it like f0, and there is no f4-SIMD.

steps.title: Task 5: which loop can be vectorized?
steps.questionText: Which of these loops can be vectorized like f0 (4 iterations at once, contiguous vectors)?

answers.text: for (x=0; x<X; x++) C[x] = A[x] * B[x];
answers.explanation: Yes: independent iterations and contiguous accesses.

answers.text: for (x=1; x<X; x++) C[x] = C[x-1] * A[x];
answers.explanation: No: C[x] needs C[x-1], computed in the previous iteration (like f4).
Yes: the constant is the same in every lane.

answers.text: for (x=0; x<X; x++) C[x] = A[x+1] - A[x];
answers.explanation: Yes: A is only read, so the iterations are independent; it needs two (overlapping) vector loads of A.

steps.title: Exercise: vectorize Base by hand
steps.description:
Base adds all the elements of V and W into sum. Like f4, sum depends on the previous iteration,
but only the final value is needed: it is a reduction, and the additions can be regrouped.
Use a vector accumulator sum[0:3] with 4 partial sums (one per lane), added together after the loop:
tmp[0:3] = V[i:i+3] · sum[0:3] = sum[0:3] + tmp[0:3] · (the same with W) ·
i = i + 4 · c = i != N · if c go back, with Alg opers/iter (S) = 4.
Simulate scalar Base (▶ Show me): {{cyclesPerAlgOp}} cycles per element.

steps.title: Task 6: your SIMD version
steps.description:
Open Edit Program, write your SIMD version of Base (the fields are filled in from the text),
save it with a new name (it is added to the list) and simulate it.
Goal: less than 1.5 cycles per element. A scalar version cannot reach it:
the two loads of each element go through P0.
Note: regrouping floating-point additions can change the rounding of the result.

steps.title: In depth: two vector accumulators
steps.description:
Your version is probably latency-bound: the two additions of sum[0:3] form a chain
of 2 + 2 cycles per iteration (Static Analysis). Use two vector accumulators,
one for V and one for W, so that the chains are independent.
Optional goal: less than 0.6 cycles per element.

steps.title: Summary
steps.description:
• SIMD processes several elements per instruction: fewer instructions per element, so the same
   processor does more work per cycle (f0: ×4 with 4 lanes).
• It pays off with independent iterations, contiguous accesses and equal data sizes;
   strides (f2) and mixed sizes (f3) need extra instructions; dependences (f4) prevent it,
   except for reductions (Base), which use vector accumulators.
When all your tasks are done, the bar shows your completion code.
